headline: Regional Water Transport and Wilderness Access
reservation: Travelers must distinguish between the Alaska Marine Highway System (ferries), which require months of lead time for cabins or vehicle space, and Glacier Bay National Park, which uses a permit system for private vessels. Commercial day tours and backcountry permits for Admiralty Island bear viewing are separate bottlenecks. Always verify current schedules with the Alaska Department of Transportation and the National Park Service.

days.title: Glacial Giants and Rainforest Vistas

stops.name: Mendenhall Glacier
stops.detail: Visit the Nugget Falls trail for views of the terminal face and watch for seasonal spawning salmon in the nearby streams.

stops.name: Mount Roberts Tramway
stops.detail: Ascend through the temperate canopy to reach alpine trails overlooking the Gastineau Channel and the surrounding peaks.

days.driving: Allow 45 minutes for local transfers; conditions vary
days.note: Low cloud cover can frequently obscure mountain views; check summit visibility at the base.

days.title: Fjords and Maritime Wildlife
days.start: Suggested: 7:00 AM from Auke Bay Ferry Terminal

stops.name: Tracy Arm Fjord
stops.detail: Navigate past granite walls and floating icebergs to reach the Sawyer Glaciers, observing harbor seals on the floes.

stops.name: Five Finger Lighthouse
stops.detail: Pass this historic aid to navigation located at the confluence of Stephens Passage and Frederick Sound.

days.driving: Vessel transit only; allow 6-10 hours depending on tour
days.note: Marine conditions in the passage can be choppy; prioritize vessels with stable hull designs.

days.title: Russian Colonial History and Tlingit Heritage

stops.name: Sitka National Historical Park
stops.detail: Walk the Totem Trail among Sitka spruce to see historic carvings and the site of the 1804 battle.

stops.name: St. Michael's Cathedral
stops.detail: Examine the distinctive onion domes and icons of this landmark representing the region's Russian history.

days.driving: Walking or local shuttle; allow 20 minutes for town transit
days.note: The park visitor center has specific seasonal hours for the master carver demonstrations.

intel.title: Roadless Connectivity
intel.text: The region is primarily roadless; movement between gateway cities requires the Alaska Marine Highway or regional air carriers. Check official ferry schedules as mechanical issues or weather can cause unannounced delays.

intel.title: Daylight Extremes
intel.text: June provides nearly 20 hours of light, while September brings the return of darkness and potential Aurora sightings. Plan activities to maximize mid-day light for glacier photography when shadows are least intrusive.

intel.title: Marine and Aviation Refueling
intel.text: Fuel availability for private vessels is limited to major hubs like Juneau, Sitka, and Ketchikan. Ensure tank capacity accounts for the long distances between protected harbors in the outer straits.

intel.title: Satellite Dependency
intel.text: Cellular reception is generally limited to town centers and often disappears once a vessel enters the deep fjords. Carrying a satellite communication device is suggested for those venturing into remote Tongass National Forest areas.

intel.title: Harbor Moorage
intel.text: In towns like Juneau, parking near the cruise terminals and ferry docks is highly restricted during summer months. Use local transit or designated long-term lots if leaving a vehicle to embark on a multi-day water excursion.

plan.arrival: Fly into Juneau International (JNU), pick up a local rental for city sights, and settle into a downtown hotel before transitioning to ferry or bush plane transport.
plan.vehicle: Standard cars suffice in Juneau or Ketchikan, but regional travel is by boat/plane; check rental policies regarding ferry transport.
plan.goldenHour: Sentinel Island Lighthouse viewpoint; light varies significantly by summer month.
